source_metadata.title: Randomized controlled trial of GenAI coach feedback efficacy, acceptability and mechanisms in anxiety worry logs

extraction_limitations: The uploaded PDF is an Article in Press unedited manuscript and explicitly warns that errors may remain before final publication.

The main manuscript states that detailed feedback framework, procedure, prompts, and examples are in Supplementary Materials; those supplementary materials were not present as attachments in the uploaded PDF, so exact prompt-level atoms could not be extracted.
Mediation values were read from rendered Figures 4 and 5; they passed structural and sufficiency validation but should receive human verification before downstream use.
Atoms are marked needs_review because no human reviewer verified this extraction.

atoms.canonical_statement: The trial evaluated the efficacy and acceptability of GenAI-generated personalized feedback during a 10-day anxiety-focused worry-log intervention relative to human-delivered feedback and worry-log-only control.

An exploratory aim tested whether changes in emotion clarity, risk perception, or behavioral engagement mediated treatment-related changes and whether these pathways differed between GenAI and human coaching.
The study used a three-arm parallel-group randomized controlled design with 1:1:1 allocation to a trained-student human coach, a GenAI coach, or no-coach control.

Simple randomization was performed in Microsoft Excel by an independent researcher not involved in recruitment, with all participants randomized simultaneously after enrollment to preserve allocation concealment.

Participants were blinded to feedback source during the intervention using post-study disclosure; they were told they might or might not receive coach feedback but were not told the source until debriefing.
An a priori power analysis specified a minimum total sample of 150 to detect Cohen f=0.15 with 80% power at alpha 0.05 while allowing 25% attrition.

The RCT was prospectively registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2500101780; April 29, 2025) and OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/YEQUX) and approved by the Tsinghua University IRB (THU-04-2025-039).
Eligibility required age 18 years or older.

atoms.canonical_statement: Participants were recruited in China through WeChat groups, official WeChat public accounts, and university counseling centers from May 2 to May 15, 2025.
A total of 169 eligible participants were randomized: 57 to human coach, 57 to GenAI coach, and 55 to no-coach control.

population.label: Randomized participants: human coach n=57, GenAI coach n=57, no coach n=55

atoms.canonical_statement: The randomized sample had mean age 22.99 years (SD 3.76), was 68.6% female, and had mean baseline GAD-7 score 8.67 (SD 4.21).

population.label: Chinese community adults with at least mild anxiety symptoms randomized to the trial

atoms.canonical_statement: All participants received an approximately one-hour standardized online group psychoeducation session with didactic content and live Q&A before starting the worry log.

population.label: Chinese community adults with at least mild anxiety symptoms randomized to the trial

concept.text: One-hour standardized online group psychoeducation with live Q&A

atoms.canonical_statement: For 10 consecutive days, all participants were asked to complete at least three digital worry-log entries per day and perform reality checks at appropriate future time points.

population.label: Chinese community adults with at least mild anxiety symptoms randomized to the trial

concept.text: 10-day digital worry log intervention with self-monitoring and reality checking

atoms.canonical_statement: Each worry-log entry captured anxiety trigger/context, somatic responses, a time-bounded specific worrying thought, distress (SUDs), estimated event probability, and anticipated consequence severity; reality checks recorded whether the event occurred and its actual severity.
All groups received daily worry-log reminders at 10:00 AM, 2:00 PM, and 6:00 PM during the intervention.

population.label: Chinese community adults with at least mild anxiety symptoms randomized to the trial

concept.text: Daily worry-log reminders at 10:00 AM, 2:00 PM, and 6:00 PM

atoms.canonical_statement: Human and GenAI coach groups received individualized feedback after 8:00 PM on intervention days 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 using five components: encouragement, worry-log summary, guidance toward short-term specific worries, reality-check reappraisal, and motivational reminders.

atoms.canonical_statement: Human feedback was delivered by six psychology students (two undergraduate, one master’s, three doctoral), none of whom had independent clinical practice experience before training.

population.label: Chinese community adults with at least mild anxiety symptoms randomized to the trial

concept.text: 10-day worry log intervention with trained-student human coach feedback

atoms.canonical_statement: Human coaches completed two-stage training including CBT-informed coaching instruction, six readings, a coaching manual, 6-8 hours of role-play with supervision, and worry-log-specific feedback practice and pilot delivery.
The GenAI coach used GPT-4 without additional training or fine-tuning and received external reference documents plus a worry-log manual as prompt context.

population.label: Chinese community adults with at least mild anxiety symptoms randomized to the trial

concept.text: 10-day worry log intervention with GPT-4-generated coach feedback

atoms.canonical_statement: GenAI system prompts defined an empathetic, non-judgmental anxiety-coach role and prohibited medical diagnosis/advice, hallucinated or off-topic content, and harmful bias while requiring grounding in specific worry-log content.

Before the main trial, GPT-4 feedback was tested on simulated worry logs and in a 10-day pilot; the first author reviewed outputs for instruction consistency, clinical appropriateness, and obvious safety concerns.

Primary outcomes were state anxiety, generalized anxiety, and pathological worry; state anxiety was measured at baseline, days 2/4/6/8, day 10, and one-month follow-up, whereas generalized anxiety and worry were measured at baseline, day 10, and follow-up.

outcome.measurement_method: STAI-State, GAD-7, and PSWQ-16 according to outcome-specific schedules

atoms.canonical_statement: Depressive symptoms were the secondary clinical outcome and were measured with the PHQ-9 at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and one-month follow-up.

atoms.canonical_statement: Feedback acceptability/alliance was assessed with six indicators: feeling heard, response accuracy, perceived encouragement, perceived empathy, emotional connection, and task-focused support.

concept.text: Feedback acceptability and perceived alliance

atoms.canonical_statement: Candidate mediators were emotion clarity, risk perception, and engagement, assessed longitudinally from pre-intervention through one-month follow-up.

atoms.canonical_statement: Risk perception was measured with a single self-constructed 0-100 item asking how likely bad things were to happen in the participant’s life over the next week.

concept.text: Risk perception

atoms.canonical_statement: Primary efficacy analyses used intention-to-treat linear mixed-effects models with repeated measures and fixed effects for group, time, and group-by-time interaction; baseline-imbalanced demographics were included as covariates.
The efficacy analysis was changed from the originally planned ANOVA to linear mixed-effects modeling; the LMM used all available longitudinal data under a missing-at-random assumption.
Complete-case analyses using the same mixed-model specifications were performed as a sensitivity analysis.
Exploratory mediation used PROCESS on a completer sample with residualized change scores, age adjustment when applicable, and bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals based on 10,000 resamples.
Baseline variables did not differ significantly across groups except age (F=3.26, p=0.04), so age was controlled in subsequent efficacy and mediation analyses.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors noted that the Chinese community sample and predominantly mild baseline anxiety limit generalizability to other cultures and to more severe clinical populations.
The authors emphasized that the mediation analyses were exploratory and require validation before mechanistic differences between GenAI and human feedback can be established.
The authors identified the self-developed single-item risk-perception measure as a threat to construct validity and psychometric robustness.
The intervention included a one-hour psychoeducation session delivered by a human facilitator, so the tested intervention was not fully automated.
The human benchmark consisted of trained student coaches rather than licensed clinicians, leaving comparative efficacy versus experienced clinicians uncertain.
The study did not systematically collect post-debriefing data on whether participants suspected GenAI involvement or their reactions after source disclosure.

Funding came from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (32200907, U2336214), Tsinghua Initiative Scientific Research Program (2022THZWJC12), and Beijing Municipal Education Commission (BJSZ2025ZD02); the authors reported no funder role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, or manuscript writing.
The authors declared no competing financial or non-financial interests.
Study datasets were not publicly available because they contain sensitive psychological intervention data; access may be requested from the corresponding author subject to research-group approval.

The authors concluded that GenAI-generated personalized feedback in this worry-log intervention reduced state anxiety and worry relative to no feedback and achieved outcomes and acceptability comparable to trained human coaches.

The authors proposed that, if replicated and extended, GenAI-augmented self-help could support a stepped-care model for lower-acuity anxiety while reserving therapist resources for higher-acuity or nonresponsive cases.
